summary: Defines the Script MIB extensibility protocol, which separates language-specific runtime systems from language-independent Script MIB implementations. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets different script-running engines plug into the same management system.

questions: what is the script mib extensibility protocol
how does an snmp agent run scripts
subtitle: A small text protocol that lets an SNMP agent hand management scripts to language-specific runtime systems.

tldr.problem: The Script MIB lets managers delegate scripts written in different languages, but an SNMP agent should not have to be built around any one language.
tldr.mechanism: SMX is a lightweight line-based protocol in which the agent sends commands such as start, suspend, resume, abort and status to a runtime system, which replies with three-digit codes and sends asynchronous notifications.
tldr.outcome: Different runtime systems, such as a Java virtual machine or Tcl, can plug into the same language-neutral Script MIB implementation. Version 1.1 is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 2593.

today: RFC 3179 is an Experimental RFC that obsoletes RFC 2593. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SMX Exists
sections.content:
The Script MIB (RFC 3165) provides a standard interface for delegating management functions: transferring scripts to a distributed manager, starting, suspending, resuming and terminating them, passing arguments, monitoring them and collecting results. It does not prescribe a language.

The Script MIB Extensibility protocol (SMX) separates language-specific runtime systems from the language-independent Script MIB implementation. The designers considered the Java virtual machine and the Tool Command Language (Tcl), and expected comparable languages to be easy to integrate.
sections.plainLanguage: SMX lets the manager stay the same while different script engines, like different kinds of workers, are swapped in behind it.

sections.title: Process Model, Security Profiles and Transports
sections.content:
A language-independent SNMP agent implementing the Script MIB talks over SMX to one or more runtime systems. A runtime system may run one script or several at once, but multi-threading is not required. Scripts travel through a local script storage area: the agent can read and write it, the runtime systems only need read access, and SMX passes the script's location so the runtime loads it itself.

Security profiles control what a script may do. An operating system profile limits what the process may use, for example the user and group identity under UNIX. A runtime profile gives fine-grained control inside a secure runtime such as a Java virtual machine or Tcl interpreter. Several OS profiles mean several runtime systems in differently privileged processes, and a runtime profile name is passed on script start. The memo suggests mapping smLaunchOwner to both kinds of profile.

Two transports are defined. A bi-directional pipe over the runtime's standard input and output is preferred for simplicity and security and needs no further authentication. With TCP, the agent listens, the runtime connects, the connection must come from the local host, and the agent must check the Authenticator in the 211 reply if authentication is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss leaves each task on a shared shelf, and each worker has its own set of rules about what it may touch. The boss and workers talk through a private tube or a local-only phone line.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
Messages are defined in ABNF (RFC 2234) and end in CRLF. The agent sends six commands, each with a transaction Id: hello, start, suspend, resume, abort and status. hello is always first and identifies and authenticates the runtime. start carries a run identifier, a quoted script file name, a security profile name and an argument. There is no compile command and no shutdown command: closing the connection means terminate all scripts and shut the runtime down.

Every reply starts with a three-digit code. The first digit is the class: 2yz permanent positive, 4yz permanent negative, 5yz asynchronous notification, while 1yz and 3yz are unused in version 1.1 and reserved for future extensions. The second digit gives the category (x1z whole runtime system, x2z scripts, x3z running instances).

Run states are the numbers 1 to 7 (initializing, executing, suspending, suspended, resuming, aborting, terminated), and exit codes run from 1 (noError) to 9 (genericError). The version string is SMX/1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss writes short notes like "start this job" or "stop that job". The worker answers with a number code, like 231 for "here is the status" or 431 for "I do not know that job".

sections.title: How Each Side Processes Messages
sections.content:
A runtime system that cannot extract both the command and the transaction identifier discards the message, and an unknown command gets 402. A generic 401 covers unlisted syntax errors. For start, it checks the run id, script, profile and argument syntax (errors give 431, 421, 432 and 433), checks that the script file is readable, starts it, then replies 231 with the current run state. Later state changes are reported with 531, and a failure before the running state ends in 538.

The agent sends start when a smLaunchStart variable is set. It starts suspend, resume and abort from set-requests to smLaunchControl and smRunControl, and also sends abort when smRunLifeTime reaches 0. For each command it waits for a reply within a reasonable timeout, and on a timeout it generally aborts the script and sets the exit code to genericError. A 401, 402 or 431 reply to suspend or resume means the runtime does not support suspending and resuming.

Asynchronous notifications include 531 for a state change, 532 and 533 for intermediate results, 536 and 537 for script errors, 538 for termination and 511 for arbitrary messages that the agent logs or displays. 533 and 537 cause the agent to generate smScriptResult and smScriptException notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side follows a checklist. If a note is garbled, ignore it or say so. If a worker is silent for too long, the boss cancels that job.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 2593
sections.content:
Messages never leave the local system. The pipe is created and connected by the agent before the runtime starts, so no unauthorized process can join it. For TCP, the critical moment is connection setup; the RFC strongly suggests that agents require authentication, especially on multiuser systems. Script files must be writable only by the SNMP agent, otherwise attackers could run arbitrary code in possibly privileged runtimes.

Compared with RFC 2593 (SMX 1.0), version 1.1 adds the 536 and 537 error replies, adds 538 to signal termination and deprecates 534 and 535, allows ':' and '_' in profile names, makes the Authenticator in the 211 reply optional, bumps the version from 1.0 to 1.1 and adds the pipe transport. The pipe was added because passing the secret through an environment variable is considered unsecure on operating systems that let users read other processes' environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the notes only travel inside one computer, it is hard to eavesdrop. The one thing to guard is the shelf where the tasks are kept, so only the boss can put things on it.
